rows: UBS Global Consumer and Retail Conference 2024
essentially full distribution in tracked channels
Celsius has emerged as a genuine third competitive force in an energy category long dominated by Monster and Red Bull, differentiated by fitness-centric, better-for-you, premium brand DNA.
Celsius launched in fitness and vitamin-specialty channels rather than convenience, building a health-and-wellness positioning before premiumizing around a 'live fit lifestyle'.
Substantial breadth-of-distribution runway: ~16 SKUs per location vs ~25 for peers; 2024 growth is about more SKUs and more facings, not new ACV.
~80% of new consumers are incremental to the energy category; consumer base is now a deliberate ~50/50 male/female split, broader than the prior female-skewed base.
Convenience is the biggest opportunity - only ~58% of tracked sales vs ~70% for peers, because convenience was Celsius's last channel entered; ~250,000 independent c-stores reachable via Pepsi.
Food service is primarily a brand-equity/marketing play - placing product everywhere people 'live, work, play' drives awareness and retail conversion.
The PepsiCo relationship is 'great' - unlocked food service and college-campus access; Pepsi provides incremental placements, coolers, displays while Celsius reps call on Tier 1/2 chains.
Energy as a category is gaining shelf space from shrinking adjacent categories (coffee, CSDs, dairy, tea, water); Celsius targets weak 'wounded gazelle' brands, not Red Bull/Monster space.
Spring shelf resets will 'stair-step' up monthly through end of May (Circle K resets in May); benefits visible progressively in two-to-four-week scanner data.
Elevated promotional spend tied to the Essentials 16-oz national rollout is deliberate 'short-term pain for long-term gain' to induce trial; expected to normalize as the year goes on.
Management reiterated belief it can reach a Monster-like ~55% gross margin and mid-30s operating margin over time, but explicitly declined to bound the timeline or give guidance.
Management is not concerned about the Bang relaunch under Monster - would be 'amazed' if Bang recaptured its prior ~10% share; will not seed back shelf space won during Bang's troubles.
Management views Celsius as economically resilient (energy held up in 2008) and a natural fit for GLP-1/weight-loss consumers given its healthy-halo, fitness positioning.
Exploring a lower-caffeine product vs the current 200 mg offering as a potential incremental SKU, but no timeline committed.
UK and Ireland launch via Suntory in Q2 2024 - the UK is one of the largest energy markets in the world; Canada launch has exceeded expectations.
In an industry dominated by two players that almost every beverage company has tried and failed to enter, what has Celsius done differently?

Kyle Watson: Celsius was 'ahead of its time,' launched in fitness and vitamin-specialty channels rather than the typical convenience route, building a health-and-wellness positioning; it then premiumized around a 'live fit lifestyle,' becoming the category's first true disruptor as a genuine energy drink with a better-for-you healthy halo while keeping its fitness-centric DNA.
Who is Celsius's core customer today and has that changed as brand awareness has grown?

Kyle Watson: the demographic is now wide; five years ago it over-indexed on females 25-40; the strategy now focuses on bringing Gen Z into the category while retaining the existing demographic, and also benefits from consumers aging out of traditional energy brands into Celsius.
Where is Celsius sourcing customers from - traditional energy consumers vs outside the category?

Kyle Watson: ~80% of consumers are increasing frequency or new to category (all incremental), ~20% taken from other brands; insights suggest pulling from RTD coffee and coffee; food service is a 'massive opportunity' given Celsius's fruit-forward, refreshing flavor pairs better with food.
What does the tracked vs non-tracked channel mix look like, and is there a target mix over the next several years?

Toby David: Celsius has not given public mix data, but ~70% of Red Bull/Monster tracked sales come through convenience vs ~58% for Celsius - not weak performance, but because convenience was its last channel entered; convenience is the biggest opportunity and also drives trial that flows to Amazon and Costco.
How does Celsius's ~12% food-service mix compare to other energy companies, and how big can food service ultimately be?

Kyle Watson framed food service primarily as a brand-equity/marketing play - touch points everywhere drive awareness and retail conversion. Toby David declined to speculate on competitors but noted Celsius is already past Bang's peak in the Pepsi portfolio; food service spans QSR, hospitals, hotels, casinos, colleges and universities.
Can you touch on the health of the Celsius-Pepsi relationship?

Toby David: the relationship is 'great,' with close work across all levels and frequent executive meetings; many ex-Rockstar/Pepsi staff at Celsius eased the transition. Pepsi unlocked food service and college campuses ('you can't get on campus unless you're in a red or blue truck') and expanded TDPs; Celsius reps still call on Tier 1/2 chains while Pepsi provides incremental placements, coolers and merchandising.
What are the US growth drivers for 2024 - TDP growth vs velocity - given ACV is high but TDPs lag the competition?

Toby David: at 98% ACV Celsius is essentially at full tracked distribution, so 2024 focus is breadth within the store - more SKUs (~16 vs ~25 for peers) and more facings; declined guidance but said the total planogram reset would stair-step monthly through May; ~250,000 independent c-stores are a massive opportunity via Pepsi.
Celsius sounds constructive on shelf resets, but so do competitors - is energy as a category gaining shelf space from other categories?

Toby David: yes - energy as a category is gaining retail footprint across the board with coffee, CSDs, dairy, tea and water all shrinking; Celsius does not target Red Bull/Monster space but rather weak 'wounded gazelle' brands not paying their fair share of cooler rent.
Within the energy cooler, is Celsius expecting better placement as well as more space?

Toby David: better placement is the objective - in regions where Celsius is still in its infancy product is often in the 'basement or the crack' with few facings; the goal is eye-level placement touching Red Bull and Monster.
When reset benefits appear in data
When should reset benefits start to appear in scanner data - coming weeks or April/May?

Toby David: March and April are big reset months; a clearer picture by end of April; Circle K (second-largest US c-chain) typically resets in May, so totality is visible by end of May, appearing as a stair-step in two-to-four-week data.
How quickly can Celsius reach mid-teens national share from ~11.5, given another 400 bps will be hard without the same distribution benefit?

Toby David declined guidance but offered color: Celsius cites Amazon and Costco for apples-to-apples comparison free of shelf constraints (#1 on Amazon); as it gains shelf space the gap should narrow; 12 markets are above 15% share, several near 20, in some of the largest US markets - a proof of concept, timing uncertain.
Is there anything about the convenience channel that would limit Celsius's ability to reach the share it sees online or in FDM?

Toby David: Celsius's 7-Eleven share is 'sizable' and larger than its national average, showing it can compete with the big players in convenience; earlier investor concern that Celsius was too fitness/female-oriented for convenience is contradicted by the data.
What is your view on the competitive landscape, including Bang coming back under Monster, and could the refresh alter Celsius's momentum?

Kyle Watson: Celsius is 'paranoid about everything,' calls the Monster-led Rain relaunch a 'huge immediate threat' but is 'not as concerned' - Rain looks like a value imitation while Celsius built a brand with loyal communities. Toby David: would be 'amazed' if Bang recaptured its prior magic; any share Bang gains likely comes from Monster/Rain or Ghost/C4, 'not from us'; the Essentials launch coincided with Bang's return - 'best defense is a good offense.'
How do you think about promotion vs advertising given the growth stage, and how to think about the international opportunity (Canada, UK, Ireland) and brand-building there?

Toby David: promotional activity picked up due to the Q4 Essentials launch (exclusive 7-Eleven, promoted nearly the whole quarter) - deliberate short-term pain for trial; with national rollout in Q1 (~40% ACV) promo spend is up short term but should normalize; Q1 gross margin will look similar to Q4. Canada exceeded expectations; UK/Ireland entered in Q2 via Suntory. Kyle Watson: brand positioning stays the same internationally, applying the proven US fitness-DNA playbook.
Gross margin near term & long-term target
Why is gross margin subdued near term, and is a Monster-like US gross margin north of 60% a reasonable long-term target?

Toby David: near-term pressure is from elevated above-the-line promotional spend on the Essentials launch; Monster's ~59% gross margin equates to ~55% for Celsius after removing hop-on-freight - a target management believes it can meet over time; operating margin target is mid-30s. Q4 S&M ticked up to 23% (from ~20%) to invest behind rapid growth vs Monster at ~9%; Monster's margin edge reflects vertical integration.
Where can the S&M line go over time, and is Monster's ~9% achievable?

Toby David: no color on reaching a Monster-like S&M profile, but Celsius can 'dial in quite a bit' over time - even 13%-14% would be a 10%+ improvement on Q4's 23%; historically 22%-24%, then ~20% for the last five-to-six quarters; spend is 'for scale, and this is to win' (Monster ran nearly 100 people in South Florida in Q4).
How loyal is an energy-drink drinker to their drink of choice, and what is the frequency for a loyal drinker?

Kyle Watson: a loyal/heavy consumer is roughly two a day (Celsius does not recommend more than two daily); much of Celsius's growth comes from increased frequency among current users. Toby David: the data-analytics team knows the competitive set and gives marketing detailed targeting marching orders.
Does Celsius need lower-caffeine SKU options vs the current 200 mg offering to increase per-capita consumption, and the timeline?

Toby David declined a timeline; a lower-caffeine product is something Celsius has discussed and is 'interested in' - potentially an incremental SKU for a second daily consumption or caffeine-sensitive consumers - but no commitment made.
Are you concerned about GLP-1 / weight-loss drugs affecting consumption?

Toby David: those drugs restrict calories and energy, so users would likely pivot to energy drinks; Celsius, with its healthy halo and fitness background, is 'the natural fit' for weight-loss-focused consumers - the industry is watching with concern 'not for us.'
Is the margin/promotion weakness because consumers are tight on budget, making it harder to drive trial of new products?

Toby David: energy is a heavily promoted category (~26 weeks/year on promotion); the lever is the depth/breadth of promotion, finding the 'sweet spot.' Celsius is not driven by the economic situation - energy held up even in the 2008 downturn. Red Bull has taken price and Celsius is watching peers, but that does not mean Celsius will take price.
